The prince of Dharma who stood up to the atrocities of

Madurai Sultanate -- Kampana Udaiyar

By Dharmavaan

May 6, 2019

This is the story of a prince -- one of the bravest sons of

Dharma -- who has been written out of the collective

consciousness of the Hindus. I hope you gain something out

of this.

Madurai -- the seat of Hindus in the south. The most

beautiful temple city. A city where Sangam literature

thrived. The sound of tiruppugazh and thiruvasagam

rendering the air in the evenings along the beautiful holy

river Tamaraparani. All this ended when the forces of the

Delhi sultantae invaded Madurai. Malik Kafur the eunuch

servant/general of Khilji invaded Madurai in 1311. The

Meenakshi Amman temple was destroyed. Only one of the

gopurams stood the remaining three demolished. Srirangam

was captured and desecrated. The Madurai sultanate was

established by Jalaluddin. The atrocities began.

Ibn Batuta, a Muslim traveled to Madurai in around 1340 BC.

He speaks thusly of the atrocities of the killed

Ghiyasuddin Dhamagani. Here are his excerpts.

The Hindu prisoners were divided into four sections and

taken to each of the four gates of the great catcar. There,

on the stakes they had carried, the prisoners were impaled.

Afterwards their wives were killed and tied by their hair

to these pales. Little children were massacred on the

bosoms of their mothers and their corpses left there. Then,

the camp was raised, and they started cutting down the

trees of another forest. In the same manner did they treat

their later Hindu prisoners. This is shameful conduct such

as I have not known any other sovereign guilty of. It is

for this that God hastened the death of Ghiyath-eddin.

One day whilst the Kadhi (Kazi) and I were having our food

with (Ghiyazu-d-din), the Kazi to his right and I to his

left, an infidel was brought before him accompanied by his

wife and son aged seven years. The Sultan made a sign with

his hand to the executioners to cut off the head of this

man ; then he said to them in Arabic : 'and the son and the

wife.' They cut off their heads and I turned my eyes away.

When I looked again, I saw their heads lying on the ground.

I was another time with the Sultan Ghiyath-eddin when a

Hindu was brought into his presence. He uttered words I did

not understand, and immediately several of his followers

drew their daggers. I rose hurriedly, and he said to me ; '

Where are you going ' ? I replied : ' I am going to say my

afternoon (4 o'clock) prayers. ' He understood my reason,

smiled, and ordered the hands and feet of the idolater to

be cut off. On my return I found the unfortunate swimming

in his blood.

Most of us cannot even comprehend this evil. A more

depraved bunch we could not envision. At that point most

Hindus had lost hope. But as always, on the side of Dharma

a warrior arose. The son of Emperor Bukka of Vijayanagara -

- Kumara Kampana Udaiyar. The warrior who would stand up

nay charge against this incredible evil. The warrior who

would risk it all to put an end to this evil and restore

Dharma.

His exploits are chronicled in Madura Vijayam an epic poem.

Legend says that he was visited by an old woman when he was

in Kanchipuram. She implored him to liberate South India

from the sultanate. More importantly, she asked him

liberate the Meenakshi Amman temple and restore its

sanctity. The prince decided. He would stand up to the

barbarians. He would rescue Madurai. He would personally

battle this evil.

This meant going to war against the barbarians and in

modern day terms a group more psychotic than IS. Bukka and

Kampana knew well what would happen to the prince in the

event of a defeat. But prince Kampana in modern parlance

was a badass -- a legendary one at that backed by Dharma.

Legend (and we Hindus for sure dismiss it as myth) says

that the prince received a sword from the goddess

Gangadevi.

Kampana began the battle. Troops of the Sultan fell in

scores and finally the sultan himself arrived to fight. In

an epic combat, Kampana destroyed the banner of the sultan,

then the bowstring of the sultan. Finally, he beheaded the

sultan. This is recounted in Madura Vijayam

The sultan incandescent with ire flung his bow and seized a

fearsome sword.

King Kampa in turn took hold of his sword sent to him by

Agastya to vanquish the king, a blade dreadful as the dark

lord of death.

Kampa riding at a great gallop lpped off the sultan's head

with his sword. The head of the sultan that had bowed to

none now lay on the ground.

A fitting end for the evil tyrants. Kampa and the other

vijayanagara Kings then restored the Srirangam temple and

finally gained possession of Madurai.

Remember this dear Hindus -- Whenever evil tries to eclipse

Dharma, whenever we feel all hope is lost there will emerge

a warrior of Dharma. A warrior so brave that the forces of

evil, however terrible they may be, crumble in his path.

Such a warrior was Kampana. Again, dear Hindus, I ask you

to take a moment to bow to this son of Dharma in reverence,

in prayer, and most importantly in gratitude. This prince

who stood up to an unparalleled force of evil. This prince

who spent his life battling for the adherents of Dharma

whose descendants (though 1 billion in number) chose to

throw him out of their collective conscious.
